extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in social institutions and American society
extracted.subtask_description: An essay-style comparative analysis of American life and institutions that examines the pleasantness of social habits and the opposing drawback of national uniformity, illustrated with examples from nature, cities, politics, and daily manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious peace and freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: No Dissenters pursue an Established Church in a spirit of watchful jealousy, nor agitate for its overthrow. Discussions on the essentials of Christianity and of theism are conducted with good temper; the sceptic is no longer under a social ban.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of tolerant relations between denominations, lack of sharp public antagonism, and general social acceptance of differing beliefs are indicators of religious peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature, heartiness, and sociability
rubrics_metrics.description: Good nature, heartiness, a readiness to render small services to one another, an assumption that neighbours or persons thrown together were meant to be friendly rather than hostile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for everyday behaviours (helping neighbours, friendly manners in travel/crowds) and a general disposition toward sociability rather than isolation or moroseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private kindness and charitable giving
rubrics_metrics.description: Nowhere is money so readily given for any public purpose; acts of private kindness — paying the college expenses of a promising boy, aiding a widow to carry on her husband's farm — and these are not done with ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure presence of philanthropy by frequency of private, modestly performed charitable acts and ready support for public causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for enjoyment and humour
rubrics_metrics.description: A remarkable faculty for enjoyment, a power of drawing more happiness from obvious pleasures, and humour as a sweetener of temper and a copious spring of charity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how readily people derive pleasure from simple amusements and the prevalence of humour as a social tempering influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit of mutual help (colonial legacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetuation of a habit of mutual help formed in colonial days: colonists needed one another's aid more constantly, being thrown more upon one another even when scattered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe cooperative practices, mutual-aid routines, and community interdependence especially in rural or frontier contexts as signs of this habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for social equality and geniality
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeling of social equality, creating respect for a man as a man, and a regard for the sentiment of the multitude which forbids standing aloof in conceit and holds up geniality and good fellowship as social virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate norms that prioritize egalitarian interactions, discourage ostentation, and reward genial conduct; note how social pressure shapes individual behaviour toward pleasantness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of natural features and landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: All the natural features of the United States are on a larger scale; through vast stretches one finds the same physical character maintained with little change — the same strata, vegetation, similar climate, long flat prairies with little variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify large-scale monotony in landscape (extensive plains, repetitive vegetation and climate) as a contributor to national uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotony and uniformity of American cities
rubrics_metrics.description: With eight or nine exceptions, American cities differ only in being built more with brick or more with wood; all the same wide streets crossing at right angles, the same shops, ice-cream stores, large hotels, street cars, locomotives — a sad monotony in external aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use built-form characteristics (grid layouts, numbered streets, similar shops and public spaces) to assess sameness of urban character; exceptions (Boston, New York, Chicago, New Orleans, etc.) illustrate contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of historical continuity in public buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence in nearly all the American cities of anything that speaks of the past; hardly any public building is associated with anything more interesting than a big party convention; history does not 'write itself in stone.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge cities by presence or absence of structures linked to long historical continuity (ancient churches, castles, monuments); lack thereof signals a novelty-driven, unhistoric urban character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of political, educational, and charitable institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Everywhere the same system of State governments, the same municipal governments; the schools are practically identical in organization, subjects, and methods though administration is decentralized; charitable institutions, libraries, lecture-courses, and public amusements are the same in type everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare institutional forms and curricula across regions; homogeneity in structure, subjects taught, and organizational type indicates institutional uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of ideas, tastes, and manners across the population
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas of men and women, their fundamental beliefs and superficial tastes, methods of thinking and fashions of talking are similar over the country; native-born Americans vary less, in fundamentals, from the dominant American type than Europeans vary among themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural uniformity by sampling beliefs, tastes, speech patterns, and mental habits across regions; note that regional differences exist but are comparatively slight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of variety and historical density (contrast with Europe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Life in Europe is capable of an intensity and richness blended of many elements which has not yet been reached in America; the web of history woven all over Europe is vast and of many colours and is fateful to every European.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider availability of varied scenes, deep historical associations, and interlinked national fortunes as enriching factors absent in a newly formed, uniform country.
